title: How many people did the Justinianic Plague kill, and did it change late antique society?
short: Ancient DNA confirms Yersinia pestis caused the First Pandemic (541–c.750), but estimates of its mortality and long-term consequences range from catastrophic to modest.
matters: Maximalist readings make the pandemic a cause of the end of antiquity: depopulation weakening the eastern Roman empire before the Arab conquests, contraction of cities and trade, and the rural and fiscal transformations of the seventh century. Minimalist readings remove that causal link and return explanatory weight to war, climate and political decisions. The answer also shapes comparisons with the Black Death and with modern pandemics, and the use of plague as a general explanation in historical narratives.
stuck: Narrative sources (Procopius, John of Ephesus, Evagrius, Gregory of Tours) give vivid but rhetorically shaped figures for a few cities, and there are almost no serial demographic records. Documentary proxies such as papyri, legislation, coin output, inscriptions and building activity can be read as showing disruption or continuity depending on the baseline chosen. Ancient DNA proves presence of the pathogen at particular sites but not mortality rates, and pollen and settlement data are often too coarse in date to isolate the 540s from other causes.
solved: A region-by-region database of dated proxies (papyri, legislation, coin issues, dated inscriptions, burials with plague DNA, high-resolution pollen cores, settlement and building chronologies) showing, with stated uncertainties, whether measurable discontinuities cluster at the documented plague waves more than expected from a baseline of other shocks, yielding bounded mortality estimates for named regions.
approach: Agents can extract and date every reference to plague waves from narrative and documentary sources, compile counts of dated papyri, inscriptions, laws and coin issues per year and region, and align them with published palaeoecological and aDNA results in a common spatial-temporal framework. Event-study statistics around each wave, with explicit baselines, would replace selective citation. Confirmation requires collaboration with ancient-DNA laboratories to screen more burials across the Mediterranean and Near East and with palynologists for well-dated, high-resolution cores.

existing.authors: Jean-Noël Biraben and Jacques Le Goff
existing.title: La peste dans le Haut Moyen Age
existing.note: First systematic chronology and map of the recurrent plague waves from 541 to the eighth century.

existing.title: The Justinianic plague: origins and effects
existing.note: Argued from papyri and legislation for major economic effects, including labour shortages and pressure on landholding.

existing.title: Famine and Pestilence in the Late Roman and Early Byzantine Empire: A Systematic Survey of Subsistence Crises and Epidemics
existing.note: Catalogue of every recorded famine and epidemic from 284 to 750, the basic reference for source attestations of plague waves.

existing.title: Plague and the End of Antiquity: The Pandemic of 541–750
existing.note: Influential collected volume presenting the pandemic as a major demographic and historical turning point.

existing.authors: Michaela Harbeck, Lisa Seifert, Stephanie Hänsch, David M. Wagner and others
existing.title: Yersinia pestis DNA from Skeletal Remains from the 6th Century AD Reveals Insights into Justinianic Plague
existing.note: Confirmed Y. pestis in sixth-century burials at Aschheim, Bavaria.

existing.authors: David M. Wagner, Jennifer Klunk, Michaela Harbeck, Alison Devault and others
existing.title: Yersinia pestis and the Plague of Justinian 541–543 AD: a genomic analysis
existing.note: Reconstructed a draft genome placing the Justinianic strain on a now-extinct branch distinct from the Black Death lineage.

existing.title: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire
existing.note: Synthesis treating the pandemic, together with Late Antique cooling, as a central cause of Roman decline.

existing.authors: Marcel Keller, Maria A. Spyrou, Christiana L. Scheib and others
existing.title: Ancient Yersinia pestis genomes from across Western Europe reveal early diversification during the First Pandemic (541–750)
existing.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116 (25): 12363–12372
existing.note: Recovered eight genomes from Britain, France, Germany and Spain, showing wide geographic reach and microdiversity of the pathogen.

existing.authors: Guy Bar-Oz, Lior Weissbrod, Tali Erickson-Gini and others
existing.title: Ancient trash mounds unravel urban collapse a century before the end of Byzantine hegemony in the southern Levant
existing.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116 (17): 8239–8248
existing.note: Dated the end of refuse disposal at Elusa to the mid-sixth century and linked it to plague and climate stress.

existing.title: Rejecting Catastrophe: The Case of the Justinianic Plague
existing.note: Argued that the textual case for catastrophic mortality rests on a few sources and maximalist assumptions.

existing.authors: Lee Mordechai, Merle Eisenberg, Timothy P. Newfield, Adam Izdebski, Janet E. Kay and Hendrik Poinar
existing.title: The Justinianic Plague: An inconsequential pandemic?
existing.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116 (51): 25546–25554
existing.note: Found no clear break around 541–544 in papyri, legislation, coinage, inscriptions, burials or pollen, and argued the pandemic's impact has been overstated.

existing.title: The 'Justinianic Plague': An "Inconsequential Pandemic"? A Reply
existing.note: Rebuttal defending the significance of the pandemic and criticizing the minimalist use of proxy data.

existing.title: The Justinianic Plague and Global Pandemics: The Making of the Plague Concept
existing.note: Traced how the modern idea of a uniform, catastrophic plague pandemic shaped readings of the sixth-century evidence.

existing.title: New Approaches to the 'Plague of Justinian'
existing.note: Viewpoint article responding to the minimalist case and reasserting evidence for severe demographic and fiscal effects.

existing.authors: Karen Hendrix, Swamy R. Adapa, Robert H. Tykot, Gregory O'Corry-Crowe, Andrea Vianello, Gloria C. Ferreira, Michael Decker and Rays H. Y. Jiang
existing.title: Bioarchaeological signatures during the Plague of Justinian (541–750 CE) in Jerash (ancient Gerasa), Jordan
existing.note: Bioarchaeological study of a mass burial at Jerash associated with the pandemic, extending direct evidence to the eastern Mediterranean.

archives.repository: Papyrological Navigator (papyri.info), Duke Collaboratory for Classics Computing and partners
archives.collection: Duke Databank of Documentary Papyri, HGV metadata and APIS images for Egyptian papyri of the sixth and seventh centuries
archives.note: Searchable texts and dates of documentary papyri, the main serial source for rents, wages, leases and legal activity before and after 541.

archives.repository: University of Wyoming College of Law, Annotated Justinian Code (Blume translation)

archives.note: Online text of the Novels used to argue for or against plague-driven labour and fiscal measures.
Major reference collection for dating changes in sixth-century coin output and weight standards.

archives.collection: Fossil pollen records, including European Pollen Database cores spanning 500–800 CE
archives.note: Open pollen data for testing agricultural abandonment and recovery around the plague waves.

archives.collection: Raw sequencing data for published ancient Y. pestis genomes from First Pandemic burials
archives.note: Reads deposited with the aDNA studies, allowing reanalysis of pathogen presence and phylogeny.

archives.repository: Packard Humanities Institute, Searchable Greek Inscriptions
archives.collection: Dated Greek inscriptions of the sixth and seventh centuries from the eastern Mediterranean
archives.note: Texts used to count dated building and funerary inscriptions as a proxy for continuity or disruption.
